claims.text: 10 U.S.C. 119(a)(1): 'Not later than March 1 of each year, the Secretary of Defense shall submit to the defense committees a report on special access programs.' Subsection (a)(2) requires, for each SAP in the budget, a brief description, major milestones, actual cost for each prior fiscal year, and estimated total cost plus five out-years.

10 U.S.C. 119(b)(1): 'Not later than February 1 of each year, the Secretary of Defense shall submit to the defense committees a report that, with respect to each new special access program, provides--(A) notice of the designation of the program as a special access program; and (B) justification for such designation.' (b)(2) adds current total program cost estimate and 'an identification of existing programs or technologies that are similar to the technology, or that have a mission similar to the mission, of the program that is the subject of the notice.'

10 U.S.C. 119(c)(2): a report on a planned classification change or public declassification of a DoD SAP 'shall be submitted not less than 14 days before the date on which the proposed change or public announcement is to occur' -- but (c)(3) lets the Secretary submit it 'at any time before' if 'because of exceptional circumstances' the 14 days cannot be met, with an explanation.

WAIVER / 'WAIVED SAP' MECHANISM. 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(1): 'The Secretary of Defense may waive any requirement under subsection (a), (b), or (c) that certain information be included in a report under that subsection if the Secretary determines that inclusion of that information in the report would adversely affect the national security. Any such waiver shall be made on a case-by-case basis.' (e)(2): 'If the Secretary exercises the authority provided under paragraph (1), the Secretary shall provide the information described in that subsection with respect to the special access program concerned, and the justification for the waiver, jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees.'

The statutory waiver in 119(e)(2) collapses the notified audience from the full defense committees to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the six named defense committee/subcommittee units -- i.e. a maximum of eight members plus the committee chairs' cleared staff, and the delivery is a briefing 'jointly' rather than a written report to the committees. This is the legal definition of a 'waived' SAP.

10 U.S.C. 119(f): 'A special access program may not be initiated until--(1) the defense committees are notified of the program; and (2) a period of 30 days elapses after such notification is received.' Note that (f) is NOT among the subsections waivable under (e)(1), which reaches only subsections (a), (b), and (c).

10 U.S.C. 119(d): 'Whenever there is a modification or termination of the policy and criteria used for designating a program of the Department of Defense as a special access program, the Secretary of Defense shall promptly notify the defense committees of such modification or termination.' This is the hook that makes each reissuance of DoDD 5205.07 a reportable event.

10 U.S.C. 119(g) defines 'defense committees' as the Committee on Armed Services and the Committee on Appropriations, and the Defense Subcommittee of the Committee on Appropriations, of the Senate; and the Committee on Armed Services and the Committee on Appropriations, and the Subcommittee on Defense of the Committee on Appropriations, of the House.

REPORTING SUNSET. The GPO text of section 119 carries the note: 'Termination of Reporting Requirements -- For termination, effective Dec. 31, 2021, of provisions in subsecs. (a) and (b) of this section requiring submittal of annual report to Congress, see section 1061 of Pub. L. 114-328, set out as a note under section 111 of this title.' The FY2017 NDAA's blanket report-sunset provision thus terminated the statutory annual SAP report and the annual new-SAP notice as of 31 December 2021.

If the sec. 1061 sunset is read as operative, the only surviving mandatory congressional touchpoints in section 119 after 31 Dec 2021 are (c) declassification notice, (d) criteria-change notice, and (f) the 30-day pre-initiation notice -- i.e. the annual census of SAPs that lets Congress detect an unacknowledged program is precisely the piece that lapsed. Reasoning: (e) waives only (a),(b),(c); the sunset note names only (a) and (b). Whether DoD continued the report voluntarily is not established by any record located here.

entities.label: 10 U.S.C. 119(e) — Waiver of SAP Reporting (the 'waived SAP' authority)
entities.desc: The two-paragraph subsection that creates the waived (unacknowledged-to-committee) special access program.

sources.name: 10 U.S.C. 119 — Special access programs: congressional oversight (full text, U.S. Code 2023 Edition, GPO)

claims.text: Verbatim: '(e)(1) The Secretary of Defense may waive any requirement under subsection (a), (b), or (c) that certain information be included in a report under that subsection if the Secretary determines that inclusion of that information in the report would adversely affect the national security. Any such waiver shall be made on a case-by-case basis. (2) If the Secretary exercises the authority provided under paragraph (1), the Secretary shall provide the information described in that subsection with respect to the special access program concerned, and the justification for the waiver, jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees.'

The waiver authority is vested in the Secretary of Defense personally and is conditioned only on the Secretary's own determination of adverse national security effect; the statute prescribes no finding of fact, no time limit, no periodic re-justification, and no congressional ability to disapprove.

Subsection (e) was in the section as originally enacted by Pub. L. 100-180 sec. 1132(a)(1) (4 Dec 1987) and has never been amended: the 2001, 1999, 1996 and 1990 amendment notes in the GPO text touch only subsecs. (a)(1), (c), (f) and (g). The waiver language of 1987 is the language in force today.

Because (e)(1) reaches only 'any requirement ... that certain information be included in a report,' a plain reading is that the Secretary may strip content out of the reports but may not skip the (f) 30-day pre-initiation notification of the program's existence. A program whose existence was never notified to the defense committees at all would therefore not be a lawfully 'waived' SAP under section 119 but an unreported one. Reasoning stated from the text of (e)(1) and (f).

claims.text: 'Waived' is a statutory term of art traceable to a single sentence: 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2) substitutes, for the ordinary committee report, delivery of the information and the waiver justification 'jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees.' Nothing in section 119 requires that this delivery be written, recorded, retained, or shared with other members.

The parallel non-DoD, non-IC statute 50 U.S.C. 3348(e) contains the same waiver test ('would adversely affect the national security', 'case-by-case basis') but a materially WEAKER carve-down: 3348(e)(2) still requires the information to go 'to the congressional oversight committees', not merely to chairs and ranking members. The eight-member floor is therefore unique to the DoD statute.

The combination that produces a genuinely invisible program is not one provision but three stacked: 119(e) removes the content from the written record; the sec. 1061 Pub. L. 114-328 sunset (eff. 31 Dec 2021) removed the annual census that would otherwise show a count; and the DoDD 5205.07 carve-out provision (see 32 CFR 117.6) removes DCSA from the contractor facility where the work is performed. Each layer is individually lawful and documented; the stack is what defeats discovery. Reasoning stated.

claims.text: Section title and scope: '50 U.S.C. 3348. Reports relating to certain special access programs and similar programs.' Codified from Pub. L. 103-160, div. A, title XI, sec. 1152, Nov. 30, 1993, 107 Stat. 1758; formerly classified as a note under 50 U.S.C. 435 before editorial reclassification.

THE COVERAGE HOLE. 3348(g)(2)(B): the term 'covered department or agency' 'does not include-- (i) the Department of Defense (which is required to submit reports on special access programs under section 119 of title 10); (ii) the National Nuclear Security Administration (which is required to submit reports on special access programs under section 2426 of this title); or (iii) an agency in the Intelligence Community (as defined in section 3003(4) of this title).' The government-wide SAP reporting statute therefore reaches none of the three communities where a legacy recovery program would plausibly sit.

3348(e)(1): 'The head of a covered department or agency may waive any requirement under subsection (a), (b), or (c) that certain information be included in a report ... if the head of the department or agency determines that inclusion of that information in the report would adversely affect the national security. Any such waiver shall be made on a case-by-case basis.' (e)(2) requires the withheld information and the waiver justification to be provided 'to the congressional oversight committees' -- with no reduction to chairs and ranking members.

3348(f): 'A special access program may not be initiated by a covered department or agency until-- (1) the congressional oversight committees are notified of the program; and (2) a period of 30 days elapses after such notification is received.'

3348(g)(1) defines 'congressional oversight committees' as congressional leadership and the authorizing and appropriations committees with jurisdiction or shared jurisdiction over the department or agency, plus the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs and the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform (now Oversight and Accountability). This definition was ADDED by Pub. L. 115-390 sec. 103(3) in December 2018; before that the statute said only 'Congress'.

3348(g)(3) still defines 'special access program' by reference to 'Executive Order 12356 (or any successor Executive order)' — an order revoked in 1995 by E.O. 12958 sec. 6.1(d), as the GPO 'References in Text' note states. The operative definition today runs through the successor chain to E.O. 13526.

entities.desc: Signed 29 December 2009, published 75 FR 707 (5 Jan 2010). Section 4.3 is the sole executive-branch authority for creating a special access program.

claims.text: Sec. 4.3(a) verbatim: 'Unless otherwise authorized by the President, only the Secretaries of State, Defense, Energy, and Homeland Security, the Attorney General, and the Director of National Intelligence, or the principal deputy of each, may create a special access program. For special access programs pertaining to intelligence sources, methods, and activities (but not including military operational, strategic, and tactical programs), this function shall be exercised by the Director of National Intelligence. These officials shall keep the number of these programs at an absolute minimum, and shall establish them only when the program is required by statute or upon a specific finding that: (1) the vulnerability of, or threat to, specific information is exceptional; and (2) the normal criteria for determining eligibility for access applicable to information classified at the same level are not deemed sufficient to protect the information from unauthorized disclosure.'

Sec. 4.3(b)(1)-(2) verbatim: 'Special access programs shall be limited to programs in which the number of persons who ordinarily will have access will be reasonably small and commensurate with the objective of providing enhanced protection for the information involved. ... Each agency head shall establish and maintain a system of accounting for special access programs consistent with directives issued pursuant to this order.'

THE ISOO ACCESS CAP. Sec. 4.3(b)(3) verbatim: 'Special access programs shall be subject to the oversight program established under section 5.4(d) of this order. In addition, the Director of the Information Security Oversight Office shall be afforded access to these programs, in accordance with the security requirements of each program, in order to perform the functions assigned to the Information Security Oversight Office under this order. An agency head may limit access to a special access program to the Director of the Information Security Oversight Office and no more than one other employee of the Information Security Oversight Office or, for special access programs that are extraordinarily sensitive and vulnerable, to the Director only.' The executive-branch oversight body for the entire classification system can lawfully be reduced to a single individual for the most sensitive SAPs.

Sec. 4.3(b)(4)-(5) verbatim: 'The agency head or principal deputy shall review annually each special access program to determine whether it continues to meet the requirements of this order. ... Upon request, an agency head shall brief the National Security Advisor, or a designee, on any or all of the agency's special access programs.' Note the National Security Advisor briefing is on request only, not automatic.

Sec. 4.3(b)(6) verbatim: "For the purposes of this section, the term ``agency head'' refers only to the Secretaries of State, Defense, Energy, and Homeland Security, the Attorney General, and the Director of National Intelligence, or the principal deputy of each." SAP creation authority cannot be delegated below the deputy-secretary level.

Sec. 4.3(c) verbatim, in its entirety: 'Nothing in this order shall supersede any requirement made by or under 10 U.S.C. 119.' The executive order expressly subordinates itself to the statutory SAP oversight scheme, including the section 119(e) waiver.

Sec. 6.1(oo) verbatim: "``Special access program'' means a program established for a specific class of classified information that imposes safeguarding and access requirements that exceed those normally required for information at the same classification level."

Sec. 1.7(a) verbatim: 'In no case shall information be classified, continue to be maintained as classified, or fail to be declassified in order to: (1) conceal violations of law, inefficiency, or administrative error; (2) prevent embarrassment to a person, organization, or agency; (3) restrain competition; or (4) prevent or delay the release of information that does not require protection in the interest of the national security.' Sec. 1.7(b): 'Basic scientific research information not clearly related to the national security shall not be classified.'

Sec. 1.7(a)(1) and 1.7(b) are the two provisions a whistleblower alleging an illegally concealed recovery program would invoke: (a)(1) makes classification to conceal a violation of law impermissible on its face, and (b) makes classification of basic scientific research not clearly related to national security impermissible. Neither carries an enforcement mechanism inside the order; the only remedy channel is the sec. 5.3 ISCAP / agency appeal process or the intelligence-community whistleblower statutes. Reasoning stated from the text.

claims.text: THE CONTRACTOR CARVE-OUT, in regulation. 32 CFR 117.6(b) (responsibilities of the Director, DCSA) verbatim: 'The Director, DCSA, will be relieved of this oversight function for DoD special access programs (SAPs) when the Secretary of Defense or the Deputy Secretary of Defense approves a carve-out provision in accordance with DoDD 5205.07, "DoD SAP Policy".' The preceding sentence establishes what is being relieved: DCSA 'Provides security oversight of the NISP as the DoD CSO on behalf of DoD components and those non-DoD executive branch agencies who enter into agreements with DoD.'

The carve-out is therefore not a classification device but an INSPECTION device: it removes the one federal agency that would otherwise physically visit, inspect, and record a cleared contractor facility performing the classified work. Nothing else in Part 117 substitutes an alternative external inspector; oversight reverts inside the SAP's own chain.

32 CFR 117.3(b) defines ACCM verbatim: 'ACCM are security measures used by USG agencies to safeguard classified intelligence or operations when normal measures are insufficient to achieve strict need-to-know controls and where SAP controls are not required.' ACCM is thus a SAP-like access control that by definition sits outside the SAP reporting statutes.

32 CFR 117.3(b) defines SAP verbatim: 'Special access program (SAP) means any program that is established to control access and distribution and to provide protection for particularly sensitive classified information beyond that normally required for TOP SECRET, SECRET, or CONFIDENTIAL information.'

32 CFR 117.23 is titled 'Supplement to this rule: Security Requirements for Alternative Compensatory Control Measures (ACCM), Special Access Programs (SAPs), Sensitive Compartmented Information (SCI), Restricted Data (RD), Formerly Restricted Data (FRD), Transclassified Foreign Nuclear Information (TFNI), and Naval Nuclear Propulsion Information (NNPI).' 117.23(a)(1) verbatim: 'The contractor will comply with the security measures reflected in this section and other documents specifically referenced, when applied by the GCA or designee as part of a contract. Acceptance of the contract security measures is a prerequisite to any negotiations leading to program participation and an area accreditation (e.g., an SCI facility or SAP facility accreditation).'

32 CFR 117.6(b) cites, as the controlling authority for the carve-out, the pre-2024 version of DoDD 5205.07 at the URL https://www.esd.whs.mil/Portals/54/Documents/DD/issuances/dodd/520507p.pdf?ver=2020-02-04-142942-827 — i.e. the 1 July 2010 directive as amended. The regulation has not been updated to cite the 12 September 2024 reissuance.

claims.text: DoDI 5205.11 (12 Sep 2024) glossary defines it: 'carve out: A provision approved by the Secretary of Defense or Deputy Secretary of Defense that relieves DCSA of its National Industrial Security Program obligation.'

The regulatory counterpart, 32 CFR 117.6(b): 'The Director, DCSA, will be relieved of this oversight function for DoD special access programs (SAPs) when the Secretary of Defense or the Deputy Secretary of Defense approves a carve-out provision in accordance with DoDD 5205.07.'

MAJOR CHANGE, 2024. DoDI 5205.11 para 1.2.i.: 'Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency (DCSA) oversight for the administration of the National Industrial Security Program will be phased out in July 2029 in accordance with the carve-out provision.' The 2024 policy therefore schedules a blanket, enterprise-wide withdrawal of DCSA from DoD SAP industrial security by July 2029, rather than a case-by-case carve-out.

A programmed phase-out of DCSA oversight across the DoD SAP enterprise by July 2029 converts the carve-out from an exception requiring SecDef/DepSecDef signature into the default state. If accurate, after that date no independent DoD agency holds a routine inspection right at SAP contractor facilities, and the record of which facilities host which programs stops accumulating in DCSA's system. Reasoning stated from 1.2.i.

The directive places the Director, DoD SAPCO 'under the authority, direction, and control of the Deputy Secretary of Defense' and requires the position be filled by 'a general officer, flag officer, or Senior Executive Service member or equivalent appointed to oversee day-to-day management of the SAP Enterprise.' The Deputy Secretary of Defense chairs the SAPOC.

WHAT MAKES A PROGRAM WAIVED, in DoD's own words. Para 1.2.f.: 'The Secretary of Defense may designate select unacknowledged SAPs as "waived" when it is determined that using standard procedures for reporting to Congress would adversely affect national security.' The waiver therefore attaches only to programs that are ALREADY unacknowledged; waived is a subset of unacknowledged, not a parallel category.

Glossary definitions verbatim: 'acknowledged SAP: A SAP whose existence is acknowledged, affirmed, or made known to others, but its specific details are classified.' 'unacknowledged SAP: A SAP having enhanced security measures, ensuring the existence of the program is not acknowledged.' 'waived SAP: A SAP for which the Secretary of Defense has waived applicable reporting following a determination of adverse effect to national security.'

WHO GETS TOLD. Para 7.2.a.(3): 'Only the chair, the ranking member, the staff directors, and one designated security manager of the defense and intelligence committees will be authorized access to waived DoD SAPs.' Para 7.2.b.: 'Members of Congress assigned to the defense and intelligence committees are authorized access to all DoD SAPs within the respective committee's SAP oversight jurisdiction, except for waived programs.'

Para 7.2.f. verbatim: 'The personal staff of a member of Congress will not be granted access to DoD SAPs.' Non-committee members and staff may be granted access only to NON-waived SAPs, and only 'by the Director, DoD SAPCO following consultation with the respective chamber' (7.2.d.). Senate and House leadership may each nominate one professional staff member for access to all DoD SAPs (7.2.e.).
BUDGET PAPER TRAIL. Para 7.2.h. (congressional budget justification materials): waived program justification material goes only to committee staff directors, not to the committees as bodies.

GAO ACCESS IS GATED. Para 7.2.g.: authorized access approval authorities may grant SAP access to GAO staff for specific projects only after the Director, DoD SAPCO consults with the chairman and ranking defense committee members. Congress's own audit arm cannot reach a DoD SAP without the audited department's SAPCO first clearing it with four members.

Para 7.1.: 'All DoD employees accessed to DoD SAPs will coordinate with and notify the DoD and OA SAPCOs through the CA SAPCO when intending to brief or provide DoD SAP material to any appropriately accessed members of Congress or professional staff member.' A cleared DoD employee cannot lawfully brief even an accessed member of Congress without first routing notice through the SAP's own control office.

PERIODIC REVIEW OF WAIVED STATUS EXISTS. Para 3.5.a.(3)(d) makes the SAPOC annual review cover 'All waived DoD SAPs to determine the need for continued waived status,' as part of the 3.5.a.(3) mandate to 'Conduct an annual review of DoD SAPs to assess the continuing need for protection of CPI within SAP security controls, in accordance with E.O. 13526 and DoDD 5205.07.'

TIER ARCHITECTURE. DoDI 5205.11 establishes a tiered SAP structure: umbrellas at tier 1, compartments at tier 2, sub-compartments at tier 3 and below; only the Secretary or Deputy Secretary of Defense may alter tier 1 structures. It distinguishes 'structural SAP: A SAP that provides organization to the architecture and does not protect discrete CPI' from 'content SAP: A SAP that protects discrete CPI.'

The structural/content distinction is load-bearing for any search of SAP nomenclature: a structural SAP is a container with a codeword and no content of its own, so a program name appearing in budget or security documentation may correspond to no discrete body of protected information at all. Conversely, discrete CPI can be moved between compartments under an unchanged tier-1 umbrella name without any tier-1 action reaching the Secretary. Reasoning stated from the 1.2 tier description.

Para 4.1.a.(2): 'Within 45 calendar days of creation of the SAP project, the CA will submit' the required documentation — establishing an internal 45-day paper deadline for new SAP projects, distinct from the statutory 30-day congressional pre-initiation notice under 10 U.S.C. 119(f).

Para 5.1.e.(1): 'The use of a polygraph examination as a mandatory access determination requirement must be approved by the Secretary of Defense.' Mandatory-polygraph SAP access is a Secretary-level decision, which makes the presence of a polygraph requirement a marker of a program that reached the top of the department.

claims.text: Header: 'Department of Defense DIRECTIVE NUMBER 5205.07, July 1, 2010, Incorporating Change 2, February 4, 2020, DoD SAPCO. SUBJECT: Special Access Program (SAP) Policy.' Enclosure 1 reference (a) records that it 'Reissues DoD Directive 5205.07, "Special Access Program (SAP) Policy," January 5, 2006 (hereby cancelled).' Releasability: 'Cleared for public release.'

GLOSSARY, verbatim: 'acknowledged SAP. A SAP whose existence is acknowledged but its specific details (technologies, materials, techniques, etc.) are classified as specified in the applicable security classification guide.' -- 'unacknowledged SAP. A SAP having protective controls ensuring the existence of the program is not acknowledged, affirmed, or made known to any person not authorized for such information.' -- 'waived SAP. A SAP for which the Secretary of Defense has waived applicable reporting in accordance with Reference (c) following a determination of adverse effect to national security. An unacknowledged SAP that has more restrictive reporting and access controls.' Reference (c) is 'Section 119 of title 10, United States Code.'

GLOSSARY, verbatim: 'carve-out. A provision approved by the Secretary or Deputy Secretary of Defense that relieves DSS of its National Industrial Security Program obligation to perform industrial security oversight functions for a DoD SAP.' And 'acquisition SAP. A SAP established to protect sensitive research, development, testing and evaluation, modification, and procurement activities.'

THE WAIVER, restated in policy. Enclosure 2, para 5: 'When the Secretary of Defense determines that national security would be adversely affected if SAP data is reported to Congress using standard processes, he or she may designate select unacknowledged SAPs as waived in accordance with Reference (c).'

THE CARVE-OUT REQUEST PATH. Enclosure 2, para 7: 'A CA may seek DepSecDef approval to relieve the Defense Security Service (DSS) of its SAP security oversight role and use DoD Component procedures instead for oversight, security review, and SAP automated information system (IS) accreditation for designated SAPs. DoD Component-designated procedures shall, at a minimum, meet the standards and frequency authorized by DoD 5220.22-M.' The requesting party is the cognizant authority for the program itself -- i.e. the program asks to be relieved of its own external inspector, and the Deputy Secretary decides.

CONGRESS KEEPS NOTHING. Para 4.h verbatim: 'All waived SAP material submitted to Congress, to include annual reports and other products, shall remain in DoD custody. No copies shall be stored outside DoD repositories or control without the approval of the Secretary or Deputy Secretary of Defense.' A briefed chairman therefore retains no document, no notes in committee custody, and no institutional memory once he leaves the chair.

Para 4.f verbatim: 'Members of Congress assigned to designated defense and intelligence committees shall be authorized access to DoD SAPs within the respective committee's SAP oversight role, except for waived programs pursuant to Reference (c). Unless approved by the Secretary or Deputy Secretary of Defense, only the chair, the ranking minority member, and the staff directors of the defense and intelligence committees shall be authorized access to waived SAPs within their committee's respective SAP oversight role.'

Para 4.e verbatim: 'All personnel accessed to DoD SAPs shall notify the Director, DoD SAPCO, in a timely fashion, when briefing or providing DoD SAP material to any members of Congress or congressional staff. No DoD contractor entity, contractor employee, contractor representative, or consultant shall provide SAP material to any members of Congress or congressional staff without Director, DoD SAPCO, approval.'

Enclosure 4, para 8: GAO personnel are granted SAP access only if 'The Director, DoD SAPCO, concurs after consultation with the chair and ranking minority member of a defense or intelligence committee' and the nominee holds the appropriate clearance. Enclosure 4, para 6: 'Personal staff shall not be granted access to DoD SAPs.' Enclosure 4, para 7 sets the annual 1 March date for DoD SAPCO to refresh professional staff access status.

Enclosure 3 (Access Approval Authority table), Note 3: 'DoD SAPCO shall coordinate on DD Forms 2835, "Program Access Request," (PARs) for judicial and other Federal agency personnel for waived programs.' Note 4: 'Director, DoD SAPCO, shall coordinate on PARs for the White House, National Security Council, and political appointees of the Executive Branch.' The AAA for the Legislative Branch is the Deputy Secretary of Defense. Judges, White House staff, NSC staff and political appointees therefore reach a waived SAP only through a DoD office that reports to the Deputy Secretary.

Enclosure 2, para 10: 'Prior to gaining access and during a period of access to DoD SAPs, all personnel shall consent to, and be subject to, a random CI-scope polygraph examination. CI-scope polygraph examinations shall not be used as the only basis for granting access to DoD SAPs. Exceptions to these requirements shall be granted only by the Secretary or Deputy Secretary of Defense.'

Enclosure 2, para 8: 'The Director, DoD SAPCO, shall annually request DepSecDef approval of the billet structure that assigns individual access by organization and duty position to the entire suite of DoD SAPs.' A single annual document approved by the Deputy Secretary enumerates every access billet across the whole DoD SAP enterprise.

Comparing the 2010 directive with its 12 Sep 2024 successor: 'waived', 'unacknowledged', 'carve-out' and the Enclosure 4 congressional-access procedures all appear in the 2010 public text and none appear in the 2024 public Directive; they now live in DoDI 5205.11. THE CARVE-OUT'S OPERATIONAL CONTENT. DoDM 5205.07 Vol 1, Enclosure 2, para 2 (Director, DSS): 'Unless a carve-out provision is approved by the Secretary of Defense or the Deputy Secretary of Defense: (1) Performs SAP security inspections at cleared defense contractor locations in accordance with this volume, Reference (f), and the government contracting activity's completed DD Form 254 ... (2) Authorizes classified contractor SAP information systems (ISs) and the introduction of guest systems in contractor SAP facilities (SAPFs). (3) Coordinates with the designated counterintelligence (CI) component to provide cross-sharing of threat and incident information affecting the security of the facility or its defense information or cleared personnel.' A carve-out removes all three functions at once: physical inspection, IT accreditation, and CI information sharing.

DoDM 5205.07 Vol 1 glossary: 'carve-out. A provision approved by the Secretary or Deputy Secretary of Defense that relieves DSS of its NISP obligation to perform industrial security oversight functions for a DoD SAP.'

Vol 1 states that inspections 'will be coordinated among the SAPCOs and DSS when not carved out and conducted jointly to the greatest extent possible' -- confirming that when a SAP IS carved out, the only remaining inspection is the program's own self-inspection plus SAPCO-internal compliance inspection.

WHISTLEBLOWING IS ROUTED BACK INSIDE. Vol 1, Enclosure 4, para 3: 'Government and industry FWAC SAP reporting involving SAP information will be accomplished through SAP channels. Collateral FWAC reporting channels must not be used for SAP information. b. The PSO will provide the telephone number for the current FWAC hotline for reporting SAP information. FWAC reporting information will be conspicuously posted in the SAP workspace. c. Employees do not need management approval before making reports.' Fraud, waste, abuse and corruption inside a SAP may not be reported through the ordinary DoD IG hotline; it must go through a SAP-channel hotline whose number is issued by the program's own security officer.

Vol 1, Enclosure 4, para 4: 'The CUA documents areas of authorities and responsibilities between cognizant security offices (CSOs) when they share the same SAPF. ... The first CSO in an area, unless otherwise agreed upon, will be considered the host CSO responsible for all security oversight.' And, critically: 'For CUAs, the responsible organization will be identified for executing security cognizance with a carved-out SAP.' Multiple SAPs -- including carved-out ones -- can lawfully co-occupy one accredited facility under a written host/tenant agreement.

Vol 1, Enclosure 4, para 7: 'PATENTS AND INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY. The CA SAPCO will develop procedures for processing patents and intellectual property involving SAP(s).' There is an explicit, standing policy channel for patents arising inside special access programs, delegated to each cognizant-authority SAP central office.

Vol 1, Enclosure 4, para 8 (Arms Control and Treaties): 'DoD SAPs will be protected against unnecessary or inadvertent exposure during USG participation in authorized verification activities, confidence-building measures, and overflights.' Para 9 (Litigation and Public Proceedings): 'Threatened or actual litigation, administrative investigations or inquiries, or public proceedings at the international, federal, State, tribal, or local levels that may involve a SAP will be reported to CA SAPCO.'

Vol 1 physical-security/visitor rules acknowledge the existence of undisclosed sites in operative text: 'Federal Government-affiliated identification cards will not be used for positive identification in unacknowledged locations.'

DoDM 5205.07 Vol 2, para 5 (Polygraphs): 'The Deputy Secretary of Defense is the approval authority for the use of polygraph examination as a mandatory access determination requirement; the requirement must be consistently applied to all candidates in accordance with DoDI 5210.91. CI-Scope polygraph examination must not be used as the only basis for granting access to DoD SAPs. Exceptions to these requirements will only be granted by the Deputy Secretary of Defense. ... CI polygraph examinations are considered current when administered within the past 5 years.' Para 6 provides that 'CA SAPCOs may establish or authorize SAP billet structures or access quotas that assign individual access by organization and duty position to SAPs under their cognizance.'

entities.desc: The Intelligence Community's counterpart to DoDD 5205.07. Current version (PDF created 19 Dec 2024, first archived 12 Jan 2025) supersedes ICD 906 signed 17 October 2015. Establishes CAPs, the CAPOC, the SRG, and the ODNI CAPCO.

claims.text: Purpose, verbatim: 'This Intelligence Community Directive (ICD) establishes the oversight and management of Intelligence Community (IC) special access programs pursuant to EO 13526, Section 4.3, or any successor document, referred to within the IC as Controlled Access Programs (CAPs). 2. This ICD supersedes ICD 906, Controlled Access Programs, signed 17 October 2015.'

JURISDICTIONAL FENCE. Applicability C.3, verbatim: 'This Directive does not apply to special access programs established pursuant to EO 13526, Section 4.3, or any successor document by the Secretaries of State, Defense, Energy, or Homeland Security or by the Attorney General, or their principal deputies. Nor does this Directive apply to special access programs under the purview of the National Security Council, such as covert action.' C.2 adds that the DNI 'may establish CAPs pertaining to intelligence sources, methods, and activities but does not have authority to establish military operational, strategic, or tactical programs.'

IC UNACKNOWLEDGED PROGRAMS. Policy D.3, verbatim: 'unacknowledged CAPs may be established only where knowledge of the existence of a program would reveal aspects of its protected information, and when there is no other means to protect information about programs at the collateral classification level, or when required by statute. Unacknowledged CAPs may be established only with the approval of the DNI or PDDNI.'

Policy D.2: 'Only the DNI or the Principal Deputy Director of National Intelligence (PDDNI) have the authority to establish, validate, modify, or terminate CAPs. For the purpose of this Directive, CAPs are defined as a top-level control system (such as Special Intelligence, Talent Keyhole, Human Intelligence Control System), and any compartment or sub-compartment under a control system within the IC.' D.2.a: 'There shall not be any levels beyond the sub-compartment levels, unless the DNI or PDDNI determine or approve otherwise.'

THE DISCOVERABILITY EXEMPTION. Policy D.5: 'Intelligence and intelligence-related information within all CAPs shall be discoverable or exempted from discovery consistent with the processes outlined in ICD 501 ... Any exemption from this requirement shall be approved only by the DNI or PDDNI, and reviewed and validated at least annually.' E.1.b lets the DNI or PDDNI 'Establish unacknowledged CAPs and/or approve non-discoverability of CAPs if a compelling case can be made that any agreed upon approach to discoverability would reveal a capability, a decision, or a fragile source, and the information contained in the compartment is so narrowly tailored, it is unlikely to be of use to officers who do not already have access to the compartment.' A CAP can thus be made invisible to the IC's own internal information-discovery system.

SCATTERED CASTLES IS THE REGISTRY -- AND HAS AN EXEMPTION. Policy D.6: 'All CAPs shall be recorded, and individual accesses to those CAPs shall be included, in the authoritative repository, Scattered Castles, or its successor system ... Any exemption from this requirement shall be approved only by the DNI or PDDNI, and reviewed and validated at least annually.' D.6.a permits access to be 'further limited by billets ... or by name or position (BYNOP).'

Policy D.7 establishes the CAP Oversight Committee (CAPOC), chaired by the PDDNI or designee, whose Chair 'shall be responsible for CAP oversight and the management of CAPs, to include all unacknowledged CAPs.' D.8 establishes a Senior Review Group (SRG) that reviews 'all CAPs, including unacknowledged CAPs' at least annually.

Policy D.9 makes the Director of the ODNI Controlled Access Program Central Office (CAPCO) 'the accountable official responsible for the implementation of this policy'; CAPCO shall 'Manage a CAP Registry that maintains a list of all control systems, including all compartments and sub-compartments ... and manage all compartment and sub compartment names, codenames, and any other pertinent information' and 'Be responsible for the coordination of CAP-related engagements, to include, but not limited to, congressional briefings, requests from the Information Security Oversight Office, and the National Security Council.' ISOO's access to IC CAPs is routed through CAPCO.

ANNUAL RE-JUSTIFICATION OF UNACKNOWLEDGED STATUS. Policy D.10.e.(1): 'For unacknowledged CAPs, IC elements shall include in their annual review submission, a justification for why each such CAP still meets the requirements to be unacknowledged.' D.10.b: 'Any new CAPs not submitted, and approved, will be terminated.' D.10.e: 'CAPs not re-validated shall be terminated and the protected information shall be de-compartmented or protected by a validated CAP.'

RECORDS OFFICER REQUIREMENT. D.9.d and D.10.g: IC elements and CAPCO must 'Ensure all records pertaining to CAPs are maintained, and ensure that at least one records official is cleared to all CAP information in accordance with EO 13526.' There must exist at least one cleared records official with visibility into every CAP.

The ICD 906 architecture is materially tighter than the DoD SAP architecture on exactly the axis that matters for concealment: unacknowledged CAPs must be re-justified in writing every year, non-discoverability requires an annually re-validated DNI exemption, and unsubmitted programs are terminated by default. The DoD side has an annual SAPOC review of waived status (DoDI 5205.11 3.5.a.(3)(d)) but no default-termination rule and no equivalent single authoritative access registry. Reasoning stated by comparison of the two texts.

entities.label: 50 U.S.C. 3091a — Congressional Oversight of Controlled Access Programs
entities.desc: Added as sec. 501A of the National Security Act of 1947 by Pub. L. 117-103, div. X (Intelligence Authorization Act for FY2022), title V, sec. 504, 15 March 2022, 136 Stat. 986. The single most significant post-2020 change to SAP-family oversight law — and it contains no waiver provision.

sources.name: 50 U.S.C. 3091a — Congressional oversight of controlled access programs (U.S. Code 2023 Edition, GPO)

claims.text: Source credit, verbatim: '(July 26, 1947, ch. 343, title V, Sec. 501A, as added Pub. L. 117-103, div. X, title V, Sec. 504, Mar. 15, 2022, 136 Stat. 986.)' -- i.e. enacted in the Intelligence Authorization Act for FY2022 carried in the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2022.

(a)(1) verbatim: 'Not less frequently than semiannually or upon request by one of the appropriate congressional committees or a member of congressional leadership, the Director of National Intelligence shall provide to such committees and congressional leadership a briefing on each controlled access program in effect.' There is no exception for unacknowledged CAPs.

(b) verbatim: 'A head of an element of the intelligence community may not establish a controlled access program, or a compartment or subcompartment therein, until the head notifies the appropriate congressional committees and congressional leadership of such controlled access program, compartment, or subcompartment, as the case may be.' The notification duty reaches down to the sub-compartment level.

(c)(2)(A)-(B): each annual report must include 'A list of all compartments and subcompartments of controlled access programs active as of the date of the report' and 'A list of all compartments and subcompartments of controlled access programs terminated during the period covered by the report.' (c)(2)(C) requires the DNI additionally to certify that the creation, validation or substantial modification of every existing and proposed CAP 'are substantiated and justified', with the rationale, an identified control officer, and a statement of protection requirements for each.

NO WAIVER. 50 U.S.C. 3091a contains no subsection permitting the DNI or an IC element head to waive, defer, or narrow the briefing, notification, or reporting duties, and no reduction of the audience to chairs and ranking members. This is the structural opposite of 10 U.S.C. 119(e).

(d)(1)-(2) define 'appropriate congressional committees' as the congressional intelligence committees plus both Appropriations Committees, and 'congressional leadership' as the Senate majority and minority leaders and the Speaker and minority leader of the House -- i.e. a statutory Gang-of-Eight-shaped audience that is a floor, not a ceiling.

(d)(3) verbatim: "The term 'controlled access program' means a program created or managed pursuant to Intelligence Community Directive 906, or successor directive." The GPO 'References in Text' note states: 'Intelligence Community Directive 906, referred to in subsec. (d)(3), is located at https://www.dni.gov/files/documents/ICD/ICD906.pdf.' Congress incorporated an executive-branch directive by reference and pointed at a URL, so the statutory scope of 'controlled access program' moves whenever ODNI reissues ICD 906.

Because 3091a(d)(3) defines its own subject matter by reference to ICD 906, and ICD 906 section C.3 expressly excludes DoD, State, Energy, DHS, DOJ and NSC covert-action programs, the strongest CAP oversight statute on the books cannot reach a program held on the DoD side of the line. Moving a program from IC cognizance to DoD cognizance moves it from a no-waiver statute to a waiver statute. Reasoning stated from 3091a(d)(3) and ICD 906 C.3.

The waiver mirrors 10 U.S.C. 119(e) exactly: 'The Administrator may waive any requirement under subsection (a), (b), or (c)' on a case-by-case adverse-national-security determination, after which the information and justification go 'jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the congressional defense committees.' Two of the three SAP reporting statutes (10 U.S.C. 119 for DoD, 50 U.S.C. 2426 for NNSA) contain the eight-member waiver; the third (50 U.S.C. 3348) does not reduce the audience, and the newest (50 U.S.C. 3091a, IC) has no waiver at all. The waiver-to-four-committee-pairs mechanism therefore exists precisely and only where physical hardware programs and nuclear-adjacent research live. Reasoning stated by comparison of the four statutes.

claims.text: DoDI 5205.11 (2024) glossary: 'acknowledged SAP: A SAP whose existence is acknowledged, affirmed, or made known to others, but its specific details are classified.' claims.text: Four statutes, each with a different addressee. DoD: 10 U.S.C. 119 (defense committees; annual 1 Mar; waiver in (e) collapsing to chairman + ranking member). NNSA: 50 U.S.C. 2426 (congressional defense committees; annual 1 Feb; identical waiver). All other non-IC agencies: 50 U.S.C. 3348 (congressional oversight committees; annual 1 Feb; waiver that does NOT reduce the audience). IC: 50 U.S.C. 3091a (intelligence committees + both Appropriations + the four congressional leaders; semiannual briefings; no waiver at all).

The seams are written into the statutes. 50 U.S.C. 3348(g)(2)(B) removes DoD, NNSA and every IC element from its own coverage. 50 U.S.C. 3091a(d)(3) defines its subject by reference to ICD 906. ICD 906 section C.3 in turn removes from its own coverage every SAP created by the Secretaries of State, Defense, Energy or Homeland Security or the Attorney General, and 'special access programs under the purview of the National Security Council, such as covert action.'

Composed, the four regimes leave two seams with no annual census obligation running to a full committee: (i) a DoD program under a 119(e) waiver, whose content goes only to chairs and ranking members and whose annual report requirement additionally sunset on 31 Dec 2021 under Pub. L. 114-328 sec. 1061; and (ii) anything protected by ACCM rather than SAP controls, which no statute names. Covert action under 50 U.S.C. 3093 is a third, separately governed channel. Reasoning stated from the four statutes plus 32 CFR 117.3.

Subsection (c)(3) permits a finding not to be reported in advance at all in extraordinary circumstances, requiring only that the President thereafter report 'in a timely fashion' with 'a statement of the reasons for not giving prior notice.'

claims.text: The Gang of Eight is a creature of 50 U.S.C. 3093(c)(2) governing COVERT ACTION findings, not special access programs. The parallel narrowing for DoD SAPs is a different provision with a different membership: 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2) sends waived-SAP information to 'the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees' -- the six units defined in 119(g), not the intelligence committees and not congressional leadership.

By contrast 50 U.S.C. 3091a(d)(2) writes an eight-person leadership set INTO the mandatory audience for every controlled access program: 'the majority leader of the Senate; the minority leader of the Senate; the Speaker of the House of Representatives; and the minority leader of the House of Representatives,' alongside the intelligence and appropriations committees. Here the eight is a floor added to committee notice, not a substitute for it.

sources.name: Public Law 118-31, National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2024 (incl. div. G, Intelligence Authorization Act for FY2024) — full text, GPO

claims.text: Pub. L. 118-31 sec. 1687(a), verbatim: 'None of the funds authorized to be appropriated or otherwise made available by this Act may be obligated or expended in support of any activities involving unidentified anomalous phenomena protected under any form of special access or restricted access limitations unless the Secretary of Defense has provided the details of the activity to the appropriate congressional committees and congressional leadership, including for any activities described in a report released by the All-Domain Anomaly Resolution Office in fiscal year 2024.' Text at 137 Stat. 621-622.

Sec. 1687(b), verbatim, carrying the note '50 USC 3373 note': 'Consistent with Department of Defense Instruction Number 3204.01 (dated August 20, 2014, incorporating change 2, dated July 9, 2020; relating to Department policy for oversight of independent research and development), independent research and development funding relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena shall not be allowable as indirect expenses for purposes of contracts covered by such instruction, unless such material and information is made available the appropriate congressional committees and congressional leadership.' This closes the IR&D indirect-cost route by which a contractor could fund UAP work without a named government program.

Sec. 1687(c)(1) defines 'appropriate congressional committees' as the congressional defense committees plus HPSCI and SSCI; (c)(2) defines 'congressional leadership' as the Senate majority and minority leaders and the Speaker and House minority leader. The notification audience is therefore explicitly WIDER than the 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(2) waived-SAP audience -- section 1687 conditions money on telling a group that a section 119 waiver would otherwise let the Secretary bypass.

Section 1687 does not repeal or amend 10 U.S.C. 119(e). It operates on appropriations instead: the waiver remains lawful, but funds in the FY2024 Act cannot be spent on a UAP-related special- or restricted-access activity that has not been detailed to the wider list. The legal question it creates is therefore an Antideficiency/appropriations question about a specific fiscal year's money, not a classification question. Reasoning stated from the text of 1687(a) and 119(e).

Sections 1687 and 7343 are deliberately mirrored across the DoD/IC seam identified in 50 U.S.C. 3348(g)(2)(B) and ICD 906 C.3 -- one addressed to the Secretary of Defense and binding this Act's funds, the other to the DNI and binding this division's funds. Section 7606(c) is the only enacted provision located here that requires a SAP-related report to go to the Judiciary, Foreign Relations/Affairs and Homeland Security/Oversight committees of both chambers -- committees entirely outside the 10 U.S.C. 119(g) 'defense committees' definition and outside the 50 U.S.C. 3091a audience. entities.label: Pub. L. 118-159 secs. 6602 & 6603 — CAP funding cutoff and the CAP-to-SAP transfer bar
entities.desc: FY2025 Intelligence Authorization Act (div. F of Pub. L. 118-159, 23 Dec 2024) amendments to 50 U.S.C. 3091a.

sources.name: Public Law 118-159, Servicemember Quality of Life Improvement and National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2025 (incl. div. F, Intelligence Authorization Act for FY2025) — full text, GPO

claims.text: Sec. 6602 inserts a new 50 U.S.C. 3091a(c), verbatim: 'Limitation on Spending.--Funds authorized to be appropriated for the National Intelligence Program may not be obligated or expended for any controlled access program, or a compartment or subcompartment therein, until the head of the element of the intelligence community responsible for the establishment of such program, compartment, or subcompartment, submits the notification required by subsection (b).' Applies only to CAPs 'established on or after the date of the enactment of this Act.'

THE CAP-TO-SAP LAUNDERING BAR. Sec. 6603 adds 50 U.S.C. 3091a(b)(2)(A), verbatim: 'Except as provided in subparagraph (B), a head of an element of the intelligence community may not transfer a capability from a controlled access program, including from a compartment or subcompartment therein to a compartment or subcompartment of another controlled access program, to a special access program (as defined in section 1152(g) of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 1994 (50 U.S.C. 3348(g))), or to anything else outside the controlled access program, until the head submits to the appropriate congressional committees and congressional leadership notice of the intent of the head to make such transfer.' Text at 138 STAT. 2507-2508.

THE TWO EXITS. Sec. 6603 adds subparagraph (B), verbatim: 'Exception.--The head of an element of the intelligence community may make a transfer described in subparagraph (A) without prior congressional notification if the head determines that doing so-- (i) is required to mitigate an urgent counterintelligence issue; or (ii) is necessary to maintain access in the event of an organizational restructuring.' Neither exception carries a deadline for after-the-fact notice, a reporting requirement, or a time limit.

Congress in December 2024 wrote an express statutory prohibition on moving a capability out of an IC controlled access program and into a DoD-style special access program without notice. That prohibition only makes sense as a response to a believed or feared practice; the statute is itself evidence that the CAP-to-SAP transfer route was live enough to legislate against. The two exceptions -- 'urgent counterintelligence issue' and 'organizational restructuring' -- are self-certified by the same official making the transfer and are exactly the two rationales a program seeking to move would assert. Reasoning stated from the text of 3091a(b)(2).

timeline.text: Pub. L. 118-31 sec. 1687 (Secretary of Defense; this Act's funds) and div. G sec. 7343 (DNI; that division's funds) bar obligation or expenditure for any activity involving unidentified anomalous phenomena 'protected under any form of special access or restricted access limitation' unless details are provided to a committee list wider than the 10 U.S.C. 119(g) defense committees, plus the four congressional leaders. Both sections also disallow UAP-related independent research and development as an indirect contract expense unless disclosed.

timeline.label: DoDD 5205.07 and DoDI 5205.11 reissued the same day
timeline.text: Both signed by Deputy Secretary of Defense Kathleen H. Hicks. The reissued Directive cancels the 2010 version and no longer contains the words 'waived', 'unacknowledged', 'carve-out' or a reference to 10 U.S.C. 119; those provisions now sit in DoDI 5205.11, which retains the glossary definitions, the para 1.2.f waiver designation, the Section 7 congressional access rules, and at para 1.2.i a scheduled phase-out of DCSA NISP oversight in July 2029.

timeline.label: Deadline passes for the SAP access-population reports
timeline.text: FY2024 IAA sec. 7606(c) required each agency head authorized by E.O. 13526 to establish a SAP to review, within one year of enactment (22 December 2023), the number of agency personnel eligible for access to such programs and report to a nine-committee list including both Judiciary Committees. No public record of any such report was located.

timeline.label: Reissued ICD 906 posted
timeline.text: The reissued ICD 906, Controlled Access Programs, carries a PDF creation date of 19 December 2024 and states that it supersedes the ICD 906 signed 17 October 2015. It requires annual written re-justification of every unacknowledged CAP, terminates any CAP not submitted and approved, and vests non-discoverability approval in the DNI or PDDNI subject to annual re-validation.

timeline.label: Congress bars moving a capability from a CAP into a SAP without notice
timeline.text: Pub. L. 118-159 sec. 6603 amends 50 U.S.C. 3091a(b) to prohibit an IC element head from transferring a capability from a controlled access program 'to a special access program (as defined in section 1152(g) of the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 1994 (50 U.S.C. 3348(g))), or to anything else outside the controlled access program' until notice of intent goes to the appropriate committees and congressional leadership -- with self-certified exceptions for an 'urgent counterintelligence issue' or 'organizational restructuring'. Sec. 6602 separately cuts off NIP funds for any new CAP until the subsection (b) notification is submitted.

timeline.label: Scheduled: DCSA NISP oversight phase-out
timeline.text: DoDI 5205.11 para 1.2.i: 'Defense Counterintelligence and Security Agency (DCSA) oversight for the administration of the National Industrial Security Program will be phased out in July 2029 in accordance with the carve-out provision.' Forward-dated commitment recorded in a 12 September 2024 issuance.

operativeAnswers.whatMakesAProgramWaived: 10 U.S.C. 119(e)(1) — the Secretary of Defense determines, case by case, that including certain information in the (a), (b) or (c) report 'would adversely affect the national security'. DoD's own restatement, DoDI 5205.11 para 1.2.f: 'The Secretary of Defense may designate select unacknowledged SAPs as "waived" when it is determined that using standard procedures for reporting to Congress would adversely affect national security.' Waived is a subset of unacknowledged.
operativeAnswers.whoMustBeNotifiedAndWhen: Ordinary DoD SAP: annual report to the six defense committee units by 1 March (119(a)(1)); new-SAP notice by 1 February (119(b)(1)); 14 days before any declassification or public announcement (119(c)(2)); prompt notice of criteria changes (119(d)); and 30 days before a program may be initiated (119(f)). Waived DoD SAP: the withheld information and the waiver justification go 'jointly to the chairman and ranking minority member of each of the defense committees' (119(e)(2)), and by DoD policy only the chair, ranking member, staff directors and one designated security manager of the defense and intelligence committees may be accessed (DoDI 5205.11 para 7.2.a.(3)); all waived material stays in DoD custody (DoDD 5205.07 (2010) para 4.h). The 119(a) and (b) annual reports terminated effective 31 Dec 2021 under Pub. L. 114-328 sec. 1061.
operativeAnswers.contractorCarveOut: 32 CFR 117.6(b): 'The Director, DCSA, will be relieved of this oversight function for DoD special access programs (SAPs) when the Secretary of Defense or the Deputy Secretary of Defense approves a carve-out provision in accordance with DoDD 5205.07.' DoDI 5205.11 glossary: 'carve out: A provision approved by the Secretary of Defense or Deputy Secretary of Defense that relieves DCSA of its National Industrial Security Program obligation.' What it removes, per DoDM 5205.07 Vol 1 Encl 2 para 2: contractor SAP security inspections, contractor SAP information-system authorization, and CI threat/incident cross-sharing. What survives: facility security clearance issuance. DoDI 5205.11 para 1.2.i schedules a phase-out of DCSA NISP oversight altogether in July 2029.
